Q: What is the difference between installing a package using pip vs. apt-get? A:

You should be aware that what makes it in the package manager undergoes some integration testing, while what is in PyPI is untested.

Q: can get metadata activity fetch data recursively at ADF pipeline? A:

When you get metadata from file stores and configure modifiedDatetimeStart or modifiedDatetimeEnd, the childItems in the output includes only files in the specified path that have a last modified time within the specified range. Items in subfolders are not included.

The output of getmetadata includes only files in the specified path to get nested values you need to iterate on output directories of getmetadata values. using foreach loop this way you can go up to 1 level deep.

@Richard Swinbank here Get Metadata recursively in Azure Data Factory document discussed the Workaround for same situation.

An alternative to attempting a direct recursive traversal is to take an iterative approach, using a queue implemented in ADF as an Array variable. You can follow above documentation to create this iterative approach.

Q: PlanCache overhead with plan-time partition pruning in PolarDB-PG A:

What is the recommended way to avoid this performance problem between PlanCache and plan-time partition pruning without applying force_custom_plan to an entire session and affecting unrelated prepared statements?

Run the statement without preparing it. The main idea behind prepared statements is to enable plan caching - that clearly just gets in your way in this case.

If you still want to wrap/alias/hide the query body, and maybe save on re-parsing it, you can use a plain SQL-language quoted-body function. It would meet all inlineability criteria meaning your calls wouldn't actually invoke a function, but rather get replaced by its body before getting freshly rewritten and planned:
demo at db<>fiddle

create function f1(date) returns setof orders stable as 
$f$ SELECT order_id, order_date, customer_id, amount, status
    FROM orders
    WHERE order_date = $1
    AND customer_id = 2222;
$f$ language sql;

explain analyze verbose 
  select * from f1('2020-01-09');
QUERY PLAN
Index Scan using orders_2020_01_customer_id_order_date_idx on public.orders_2020_01 orders (cost=0.29..8.31 rows=1 width=34) (actual time=0.006..0.008 rows=3 loops=1)

  Output: orders.order_id, orders.order_date, orders.customer_id, orders.amount, orders.status

  Index Cond: ((orders.customer_id = 2222) AND (orders.order_date = '2020-01-09'::date))
Planning Time: 0.111 ms
Execution Time: 0.017 ms

There's no mention of f1 in the plan because that's the plan of the query taken out of f1, that got inlined.

Although calling SELECT (f1('2020-01-09')).*; for a RETURNING SETOF orders, or a SELECT f1('2020-01-09'); for a RETURNING TABLE function would return the same result, it needs to stay down in the FROM section to enable inlining.

Functions let you attach custom config overrides:

| SET configuration_parameter { TO value | = value | FROM CURRENT }

configuration_parameter
value

The SET clause causes the specified configuration parameter to be set to the specified value when the function is entered, and then restored to its prior value when the function exits. SET FROM CURRENT saves the value of the parameter that is current when CREATE FUNCTION is executed as the value to be applied when the function is entered.

PL/pgSQL implicit query plan caching is mentioned in the plan_cache_mode doc entry - if you wrap your query in that and set it accordingly, you'll get your desired method of defining plan caching behaviour for specific (sets of) queries, whenever you can't get them inlined. Otherwise, PL/pgSQL comes with a bit of overhead you don't need - these are query times from 30k loops from the demo.

variant avg min max sum stddev mode
f1_setof_sql 0.000109 0.000096 0.023036 3.267045 0.00015 0.000102
f3_setof_plpgsql 0.000115 0.000102 0.006454 3.447787 0.000055 0.000109
f2_table_sql 0.000116 0.000102 0.016767 3.475205 0.000117 0.000109
f4_table_plpgsql 0.000118 0.000105 0.006379 3.554796 0.000071 0.000111

PostgreSQL version 18 brought some plan caching improvements for non-inlineable plain SQL-language functions as well as query planning on partitioned tables in general. According to PolarDB's Major version feature comparison, PostgreSQL 18 is available, so you can consider an upgrade.

Q: Query filters are duplicating SQL A:

You can solve this by using database views:

CREATE VIEW v_car_model AS
  SELECT c.*, b.resourceid
  FROM carmodel c
  JOIN brand b ON b.id = c.brandid;

Then revoke direct access to the car table and grant access to the view instead.

Thus

modelBuilder.Entity<CarModel>()
    .HasQueryFilter(x =>
        x.Brand.ResourceId != null &&
        AllowedResourceIds.Contains(x.Brand.ResourceId));

will become a simple

modelBuilder.Entity<CarModel>()
    .HasQueryFilter(x =>
        x.ResourceId != null &&
        AllowedResourceIds.Contains(x.ResourceId));

If users log in to the database with an account of their own (i.e. not a shared account), you could even store users' resource IDs in the database and have the DBMS handle the access rights:

CREATE VIEW v_brand AS
  SELECT *
  FROM brand
  WHERE ressourceid IN (SELECT ur.ressourceid
                          FROM user_ressource ur
                          WHERE ur.user_name = USER);

CREATE VIEW v_car_model AS
  SELECT *
  FROM carmodel
  WHERE brandid IN (SELECT vb.id FROM v_brand vb);

If possible, this is the option I prefer, for it makes it impossible for any app to ever get data out of the database the user is not allowed to see.

Q: Convert typedef struct from C++ to Python A:

The analog to typedef in c/c++ but in Python is just TypeAlias. Like that:
typedef unsigned int uint; //c
uint = int // Python -> just a simple assignment
or, for Types Annotations is
from typing import TypeAlias

UserId: TypeAlias = int
and then use it:
user_id: UserId = 123
So, for your Word structure alias type use
from typing import TypeAlias
word: TypeAlias = Word
